sources.title: Herdr: Install; One Rust binary
sources.finding: Herdr TUI runs as a Rust terminal program with a product CLI on macOS, Linux and Windows; it is not an Electron desktop client.

sources.title: Herdr: Questions: How is it different; Which systems
sources.locator: Questions: How is it different; Which systems
sources.finding: The new Herdr native app supports Apple silicon macOS, Linux x86_64 and ARM64, and Windows x86_64. It is separate from TUI and does not share its running agents.

sources.title: Herdr: Supported agents
sources.finding: Herdr TUI runs existing agent CLIs in real terminal panes. Documented detections include Claude Code, Codex, Cursor Agent CLI, OpenCode, Pi, Grok CLI and Gemini CLI, with Gemini state detection labeled less tested. Other commands run as plain terminals.

sources.title: Herdr: Install
sources.finding: Install the Herdr binary or a package-manager build, start it where the repository lives and run existing agent commands. Saved SSH machines connect to their own server.

sources.title: Herdr: Choose an integration layer; What you can control
sources.locator: Choose an integration layer; What you can control
sources.finding: Herdr provides CLI wrappers and a local socket API for workspaces, tabs, panes, agent prompts, waits, state events and integration management. The binary emits its matching JSON schema.

sources.title: Herdr: Plugins
sources.finding: Plugins extend Herdr terminal panes and workflows, with a marketplace and CLI/API management. This does not establish a built-in MCP client.

sources.title: Herdr: One Rust binary
sources.finding: Herdr TUI is a Rust binary running in the user terminal rather than an Electron app. This implementation statement does not describe the newer native app.

sources.title: Herdr: What you can control
sources.finding: Scripts and agents create and name workspaces, tabs and panes. These are terminal sessions rather than evidence of persistent native issue objects.

sources.title: Herdr: Snapshot restore
sources.finding: Saved session shape retains workspaces, tabs, panes, current directories, layout, focus and supported native agent session references. Agent reasoning memory remains harness-owned.

sources.title: Herdr: Agents; State rollups
sources.finding: Multiple agent terminals run concurrently; working, blocked, done and idle states roll up into tabs and workspaces. Observed concurrency and quotas remain untested.

sources.title: Herdr: Raw methods
sources.finding: Agents and scripts can start, prompt and wait on selected panes. agent.prompt refuses to send input when the resolved agent is already blocked. This is pane dispatch rather than task ownership enforcement.

sources.title: Herdr: What you can control; Raw methods
sources.locator: What you can control; Raw methods
sources.finding: Herdr supplies agent start, read, prompt and event-driven wait operations to external agents and scripts. A wait pins the current pane occupant; Herdr does not thereby become a product-owned reasoning coordinator.

sources.title: Herdr: Supported agents; Blocked state
sources.finding: Known agents report or are detected as idle, working or blocked, with notifications when they finish or need input. Detection can fall back to idle for unfamiliar prompts; that is not permission to approve.

sources.title: Herdr: State rollups
sources.finding: The sidebar rolls a blocked pane up to its tab and workspace, and shows active work and done agents until viewed. No six-task fleet scenario was run.

sources.title: Herdr: CLI examples
sources.finding: Users can start one terminal task, split panes, prompt agents and wait on their state through the same CLI/socket control API.

sources.title: Herdr: Connecting machines
sources.finding: Local and saved SSH machines each own their server, sessions and processes. SSH interruptions leave remote work running; clients reconnect independently. The user supplies and pays for the host.

sources.title: Herdr: Raw methods: Worktree
sources.finding: The TUI socket exposes worktree.list, worktree.create, worktree.open and worktree.remove with workspace provenance. Git worktrees separate checkouts; no hostile-code containment is claimed.

sources.title: Herdr: What survives; Snapshot restore; Native agent session restore
sources.locator: What survives; Snapshot restore; Native agent session restore
sources.finding: Detach keeps original processes alive. Server restart loses processes but restores layout, and supported integrations can resume native conversations. Optional pane screen replay is off by default; experimental live handoff is best effort.

sources.title: Herdr: Snapshot restore
sources.finding: Restored panes return to saved directories or remain visibly errored if the directory or shell is unavailable. Snapshot restore does not recreate arbitrary services or test processes.

sources.title: Herdr: Raw methods: agent.wait
sources.finding: Agent waits have explicit until and timeout_ms controls; an atomic prompt-and-wait avoids the race between separate operations. These are wait limits, not provider token or spend controls.

sources.title: Herdr: How status works; Blocked state; Detection manifests
sources.locator: How status works; Blocked state; Detection manifests
sources.finding: State derives from screen manifests or integration reports. herdr agent explain exposes matched rules, source/version and idle fallback reasons. A process failure/approval fixture has not been induced.

sources.title: Herdr: Saved data; Updates
sources.finding: Remote connection authentication stays with OpenSSH. Saved machine profiles contain labels, target and session, but not passwords or private keys. This does not establish organization roles or SSO.

sources.title: Herdr: Pane screen history replay
sources.finding: Optional pane history stores recent terminal output locally and may contain secrets. It is disabled by default and is not an immutable audit log.

sources.title: Herdr: State rollups
sources.finding: The sidebar helps find agents needing attention and jump to the relevant terminal. A product code-diff review interface was not established.

sources.title: Herdr TUI: CLI reference
sources.locator: herdr agent attach; herdr terminal attach
sources.finding: Herdr TUI lets one client own a terminal at a time; herdr agent attach and terminal attach accept --takeover to replace the current owner. It is terminal input ownership, not verified authorized colleague workflow takeover.

sources.title: Herdr: Pane screen history replay
sources.finding: Optional local pane-history replay preserves recent terminal contents after restart. A task/revision-linked artifact library was not found.

sources.locator: skills/herdr/SKILL.md, sections on panes and agents
sources.finding: The shipped skill tells an agent running inside a Herdr pane to use the herdr CLI to inspect neighbouring work, start agents and commands in panes, send input, read output and wait for agent states such as idle, working, blocked and done. sources.title: Herdr core security boundaries
sources.locator: What runs; Who can connect; Remote trust
sources.finding: Core runs commands with the OS account access and explicitly is not a sandbox. There is no API password or per-client permission check; SSH supplies login and core does not authenticate a remote user. This establishes no product-owned roles or enterprise SSO.

sources.title: Herdr native capability boundary inspection
sources.locator: TUI src/api and src/state at 2ecf19a; native app src and defaults at 69ba1ca; core crates/herdr-core/src and schema/released.openrpc.json at d9e6826. Searches: issue, backlog, schedule, cron, webhook, pull request, SSO, RBAC.
sources.finding: The inspected built-in APIs and persisted records organize machines, terminal sessions, workspaces and panes, with no standalone issue catalog, native schedule/webhook trigger service or PR lifecycle operations. User scripts and mods can supply external integrations.

sources.title: Herdr native Changes panel
sources.locator: Shipped Changes mod lines 75-138; CHANGELOG.md records Changes diff fixes in the released app
sources.finding: The native app ships a Changes panel that lists changed files and additions/deletions, runs git diff against HEAD and renders selected-file hunks. It limits previews to 1500 lines and reports binary or unreadable files. This is a native-app feature, separate from the TUI.
